questions.stem: Muons are produced high in the atmosphere and many reach the ground. Why is this a problem for classical physics?
options: Classically they should be deflected away from Earth by the Sun's gravity
Their charge should classically make them stick to air molecules high up
Their lifetime at rest is so short that classically few should survive the trip
Classically they should travel faster than light by the time they reach the ground
questions.explanation: A muon at rest lives about 2.2 µs on average. Even moving close to c, classical physics says it would cover well under a kilometre in that time, so very few should reach the ground from many kilometres up. Far more arrive than this predicts, which special relativity explains.

questions.stem: In a particle accelerator, electrons already moving at 0.99c are given much more energy. Their momentum rises greatly, but their speed hardly changes. Why can classical physics not explain this?
options: Classically the electrons should lose momentum as they gain energy
Classically the electrons should stop moving once they reach the speed of light
Classically momentum is not conserved for charged particles in a field
Classically p = mv, so momentum could only rise greatly if the speed did too
questions.explanation: In classical physics momentum is mass times velocity, so a large gain in momentum requires a large gain in speed, and nothing stops a particle passing c. Measured momentum instead follows p = m₀v/√(1 − v²/c²), which rises without limit as v approaches c.

questions.stem: Which of these is, to a good approximation, an inertial frame of reference?
options: A lift speeding up as it leaves the ground floor
A rocket accelerating upward during launch
A train moving at constant velocity on a straight track
A car rounding a bend at a constant speed
questions.explanation: An inertial frame is one that is not accelerating, where Newton's first law holds. A train at constant velocity on straight track qualifies. A car on a bend is accelerating because its direction changes, even at constant speed.

questions.stem: Which statement is one of Einstein's two postulates of special relativity?
options: Mass and energy are equivalent, related by E = mc²
Moving clocks are measured to run slow by stationary observers
There is a fixed frame of reference in which light travels at c
The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers
questions.explanation: The two postulates are that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers. Mass-energy equivalence and time dilation are consequences derived from the postulates, not postulates themselves.

questions.stem: A passenger walks towards the front of a train at 1.5 m s⁻¹ while the train moves at 20 m s⁻¹ past a platform. What is the passenger's true speed?
options: 1.5 m s⁻¹, because the passenger's own frame is the true one
20 m s⁻¹, because the passenger's walking speed is too small to count
Neither value; speed has meaning only relative to a chosen frame
21.5 m s⁻¹, because the platform is the true frame of reference
questions.explanation: The passenger moves at 1.5 m s⁻¹ relative to the train and about 21.5 m s⁻¹ relative to the platform, and both are equally valid. By the first postulate no inertial frame is special, so motion can only be measured relative to an observer.

questions.stem: Two spacecraft drift past each other at constant velocity in deep space. Each crew says it is at rest and the other ship is moving. Who is correct?
options: The crew of the heavier ship, because it has more inertia
The crew that measures the speed of light more accurately
Both, because no experiment can single out one frame as truly at rest
Neither, because both ships are really moving relative to the stars
questions.explanation: By the first postulate, the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, so no experiment either crew does can show which is 'really' moving. Each crew is entitled to treat itself as at rest. Both crews measure the same speed of light.

questions.stem: A light clock bounces a light pulse between two mirrors. An observer watches the clock move sideways past at high speed. Why does she measure each tick as longer than the clock's owner does?
options: The pulse travels faster but must cover a much longer path
The pulse follows a longer diagonal path at the same speed c
The pulse travels more slowly because the clock is moving
The mirrors move further apart because of the clock's speed
questions.explanation: In the observer's frame the mirrors move sideways while the light is in flight, so the pulse travels a longer diagonal path. Light moves at c in every inertial frame, so a longer path takes longer, and each tick is dilated. The mirror separation is perpendicular to the motion, so it is not contracted.

questions.stem: Which quantity do all inertial observers measure to have the same value, whatever their motion?
options: The time between two separated events
The length of a moving rod
The momentum of a moving particle
The speed of light in a vacuum
questions.explanation: The second postulate says every inertial observer measures the same speed of light in a vacuum. Time intervals, lengths along the motion and momentum all depend on the observer's frame, which is why time dilation and length contraction occur.

questions.stem: What does the relativity of simultaneity mean?
options: Two events that happen together in one frame happen together in every frame
Two events can only be simultaneous if they happen at the same place
Clocks in moving frames run fast compared with stationary clocks
Events simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another
questions.explanation: Because light travels at c in every frame, observers in relative motion can disagree about whether two separated events happen at the same time. Neither observer is wrong; simultaneity depends on the frame. Events at the same place and time are simultaneous in all frames.

questions.stem: A lamp at the exact centre of a moving train carriage flashes once. A passenger sees the light reach the front and rear walls at the same time. What does an observer on the platform see?
options: The light reaches the front wall first
The light reaches both walls at the same time
The light travels faster towards the front wall
The light reaches the rear wall first
questions.explanation: On the platform, light still travels at c in both directions, but the rear wall moves towards the flash and the front wall moves away from it. The light therefore reaches the rear wall first. The light does not travel faster towards the front, which is why the observers disagree about simultaneity.

questions.stem: Lightning strikes the front and back of a moving train at the same time according to an observer standing on the platform midway between the strikes. What does a passenger at the middle of the train conclude?
options: The strikes cannot be ordered by anyone on the train
The strike at the front happened first
The strike at the back happened first
Both strikes happened at the same time
questions.explanation: The passenger moves towards the light from the front strike and away from the light from the back, so the front flash reaches her first. Light travels at c in her frame and she is at the midpoint of the train, so she concludes the front strike really happened first. Each observer is correct in their own frame.

questions.stem: According to special relativity, how does an observer measure a clock that is moving relative to her?
options: It stops completely once it passes half the speed of light
It runs slow compared with her own clocks
It runs fast compared with her own clocks
It runs at exactly the same rate as her own clocks
questions.explanation: Time dilation means a moving clock is measured to tick more slowly than identical clocks at rest in the observer's frame, by the factor √(1 − v²/c²). The effect grows smoothly with speed; a moving clock never stops.

questions.stem: The proper time interval between two events is the interval measured by:
options: an observer for whom both events happen at the same place
an observer who is at rest relative to the Earth's surface
an observer for whom the two events are furthest apart
any observer who uses a sufficiently accurate atomic clock
questions.explanation: Proper time is measured in the frame where the two events occur at the same location, such as by a clock travelling with a particle. Every other inertial observer measures a longer, dilated interval. Being at rest on Earth does not make a frame special.

questions.stem: An astronaut travels at 0.80c relative to Earth. Her ship's clock records the trip as 3.0 years. How long does it take according to clocks on Earth?
options: 1.8 years
3.0 years
8.3 years
5.0 years
questions.explanation: The ship's clock measures proper time, t₀ = 3.0 years. Then t = t₀/√(1 − v²/c²) = 3.0/√(1 − 0.64) = 3.0/0.60 = 5.0 years. Multiplying by 0.60 instead of dividing gives 1.8 years, and dividing by 0.36, forgetting the square root, gives 8.3 years.

questions.stem: A spacecraft travels at 0.28c, where √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.96. A meal on board takes 1.00 hour by the crew's clock. How long does it last according to an observer on Earth?
options: 1.04 hours
0.96 hours
1.00 hours
1.28 hours
questions.explanation: The crew measures proper time, so the Earth observer measures t = 1.00/0.96 ≈ 1.04 hours. Multiplying by 0.96 instead gives 0.96 hours, a contraction rather than a dilation. The effect is small at 0.28c, but not zero.

questions.stem: A charged pion has a mean lifetime of 2.6 × 10⁻⁸ s in its own frame. In a laboratory it moves at 0.98c, where √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.20. On average, how far does it travel in the laboratory before decaying? Use c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: In the lab its lifetime is dilated to 2.6 × 10⁻⁸ / 0.20 = 1.3 × 10⁻⁷ s, so it travels 0.98 × 3.0 × 10⁸ × 1.3 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 38 m. Using the proper lifetime gives only 7.6 m, and dividing that by 5 instead of multiplying gives 1.5 m.

questions.stem: In 1971 Hafele and Keating flew caesium atomic clocks around the world on commercial aircraft and compared them with clocks left on the ground. What did the experiment show?
options: The clocks differed by several seconds, far more than relativity predicted
The clocks differed by amounts that agreed with the predictions of relativity
The clocks agreed exactly, showing time is the same in every frame
The flown clocks gained time in both directions, unlike relativity's predictions
questions.explanation: After the flights, the airborne clocks differed from the ground clocks by tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, consistent with relativity's predictions of time dilation. The effects were tiny but measurable with atomic clocks, giving direct evidence that moving clocks run at different rates.

questions.stem: How does special relativity explain, in Earth's frame, why so many muons reach the ground?
options: The atmosphere is contracted in Earth's frame, so the distance is shorter
They travel faster than light, so they cover the distance in time
Their lifetimes are dilated, so they survive long enough to travel the distance
Their lifetimes are shortened, so they decay only after reaching the ground
questions.explanation: In Earth's frame the fast-moving muons' internal clocks run slow, so their mean lifetime is many times longer than 2.2 µs and many survive the trip. Length contraction of the atmosphere is the explanation in the muon's frame, not Earth's. Muons travel close to c, never faster.

questions.stem: A metre rule lies along the floor of a train moving at high speed past a platform. Who measures the rule's proper length?
options: An observer moving faster than the train in the same direction
A passenger on the train, at rest relative to the rule
An observer standing still on the platform beside the track
Any observer, as all observers agree on the rule's length
questions.explanation: Proper length L₀ is measured in the object's rest frame, so the passenger on the train measures it, and it is the longest length anyone measures. The platform observer sees the rule moving along its length and measures it contracted. Observers in relative motion do not agree on lengths along the motion.

questions.stem: A rod moving lengthwise at 0.866c, where √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.50, is measured as 2.0 m long by a stationary observer. What is its proper length?
questions.explanation: L = L₀√(1 − v²/c²), so L₀ = L/0.50 = 4.0 m. The measured 2.0 m is the contracted length, so the proper length must be longer. Multiplying by 0.50 instead gives 1.0 m, which treats 2.0 m as the proper length.

questions.stem: A spacecraft with a proper length of 150 m passes an observer at 0.80c, where √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.60. What length does the observer measure?
questions.explanation: L = L₀√(1 − v²/c²) = 150 × 0.60 = 90 m. Dividing by 0.60 gives 250 m, but moving objects are measured shorter, never longer. Multiplying by 0.36, forgetting the square root, gives 54 m.

questions.stem: A spacecraft is measured by an observer to be half its proper length. How fast is it moving relative to the observer?
questions.explanation: √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.50, so 1 − v²/c² = 0.25 and v²/c² = 0.75, giving v = √0.75 c ≈ 0.87c. Stopping at v²/c² = 0.75 gives 0.75c, and assuming the contraction factor equals v/c gives 0.50c.

questions.stem: A cube moves past an observer at high speed, parallel to one of its edges. How does its shape appear in the observer's frame?
options: Shorter in all three dimensions, keeping a cube shape
Longer along its direction of motion, unchanged across it
Unchanged, because length contraction is only an illusion
Shorter along its direction of motion, unchanged across it
questions.explanation: Length contraction happens only along the direction of relative motion; lengths perpendicular to the motion are unchanged. The cube is measured as a box that is shorter in the direction it travels. The contraction is a real result of measurement in that frame, not an optical illusion.

questions.stem: What is the rest mass of a particle?
options: The mass of a particle that has been brought to absolute zero
Its mass measured in a frame in which it is at rest
Its mass when it is moving close to the speed of light
The mass it loses when it comes to rest after a collision
questions.explanation: Rest mass m₀ is the mass measured by an observer at rest relative to the particle. It is the same for all observers, and it is the mass used in the relativistic momentum formula p = m₀v/√(1 − v²/c²).

questions.stem: An electron moves at 0.80c, where √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.60. What is its relativistic momentum? Use electron rest mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
options: 1.3 × 10⁻²² kg m s⁻¹
6.1 × 10⁻²² kg m s⁻¹
3.6 × 10⁻²² kg m s⁻¹
2.2 × 10⁻²² kg m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: p = m₀v/√(1 − v²/c²) = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.40 × 10⁸ / 0.60 ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻²² kg m s⁻¹. The classical value m₀v is 2.2 × 10⁻²², multiplying by 0.60 gives 1.3 × 10⁻²², and dividing by 0.36 gives 6.1 × 10⁻²².

questions.stem: A proton moves at 0.60c, where √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.80. By what factor is its relativistic momentum greater than the classical value m₀v?
questions.explanation: The relativistic momentum is m₀v divided by √(1 − v²/c²), so the factor is 1/0.80 = 1.25. The value 0.80 is the square root itself, and 1.56 = 1/0.64 comes from forgetting the square root.

questions.stem: A graph shows a particle's momentum against its speed, up to speeds close to c. How does the relativistic curve compare with the classical straight line p = m₀v?
options: It matches at all speeds, because relativistic effects are too small to see
It lies below the classical line, levelling off at a maximum momentum
It curves upward at low speeds, then becomes a straight line near c
It matches at low speeds, then curves upward without limit as v nears c
questions.explanation: At low speeds √(1 − v²/c²) is almost exactly 1, so relativistic and classical momentum agree. As v approaches c the factor falls towards zero, so the momentum rises steeply and without limit. The curve never reaches c.

questions.stem: A constant net force acts on a proton for a very long time. What happens to its momentum and speed?
options: Its momentum and speed both rise steadily until it passes the speed of light
Its momentum stops rising once its speed gets close to the speed of light
Its speed keeps rising steadily, while its momentum levels off near a limit
Its momentum keeps rising steadily, while its speed approaches but never reaches c
questions.explanation: A constant force changes momentum at a constant rate, since F = Δp/Δt, so the momentum keeps increasing. Because p = m₀v/√(1 − v²/c²) grows without limit as v approaches c, ever larger momentum corresponds to ever smaller gains in speed, and c is never reached.

questions.stem: What is the main implication of relativistic momentum increasing without limit as an object's speed approaches c?
options: Light must have an extremely large rest mass to travel at c
Momentum is not conserved in collisions at very high speeds
No object with mass can be accelerated to the speed of light
Objects with mass can exceed c if a large enough force is applied
questions.explanation: Reaching c would require infinite momentum, and so an infinite impulse and infinite energy, which is impossible. So c is a speed limit for anything with mass. Momentum is still conserved at high speeds, provided the relativistic expression is used.

questions.stem: What does the mass-energy equivalence relationship ΔE = Δmc² state?
options: Energy and mass are both conserved separately in every process
Mass can be converted to energy only at the speed of light
A change in a system's energy corresponds to a change in its mass
Only nuclear reactions can convert mass into energy
questions.explanation: Mass is a form of energy, so any change in a system's energy, whether nuclear, chemical, thermal or elastic, comes with a change in its mass of ΔE/c². The effect is only measurable for large energy changes, such as in nuclear reactions, because c² is so large.

questions.stem: A uranium-235 nucleus releases about 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J when it undergoes fission. What mass is converted into this energy? Use c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Δm = ΔE/c² = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ / (3.0 × 10⁸)² ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻²⁸ kg. Dividing by c instead of c² gives 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg, and multiplying by c² gives 2.9 × 10⁶ kg.

questions.stem: How much energy would be released if 2.0 g of mass were converted entirely into energy? Use c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: ΔE = Δmc² = 2.0 × 10⁻³ × (3.0 × 10⁸)² = 1.8 × 10¹⁴ J. Leaving the mass in grams gives 1.8 × 10¹⁷ J, and multiplying by c instead of c² gives 6.0 × 10⁵ J.

questions.stem: A spring is compressed, storing 50 J of elastic potential energy. How does its mass change? Use c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
options: It increases by about 1.7 × 10⁻⁷ kg
It increases by about 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ kg
It stays exactly the same, as no matter is added
It decreases by about 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ kg
questions.explanation: The stored energy adds to the spring's mass: Δm = ΔE/c² = 50/(9.0 × 10¹⁶) ≈ 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ kg. This is far too small to measure, but mass-energy equivalence applies to all energy, not just nuclear energy. Dividing by c instead of c² gives 1.7 × 10⁻⁷ kg.

questions.stem: In the twins' paradox, one twin travels to a distant star at high speed and returns. Why is it the travelling twin who is younger on return, and not the other way round?
options: Each twin is younger in their own frame, so both are younger when they meet again
The travelling twin changes inertial frames by turning around, so the situation is not symmetrical
The travelling twin is the one moving, and moving people always age more slowly than others
The Earth twin's clock runs fast because Earth's gravity speeds up time on its surface
questions.explanation: Each twin sees the other's clock run slow while they move apart at constant velocity, but only the traveller accelerates and turns around, switching inertial frames. That breaks the symmetry, and when the twins meet at one place they agree the traveller has aged less. Motion alone cannot decide it, since motion is relative.

questions.stem: A twin travels at 0.80c, where √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.60, to a star 4.0 light-years from Earth and straight back. How much does each twin age during the trip?
options: Earth twin 10 years; travelling twin 10 years
Earth twin 6.0 years; travelling twin 10 years
Earth twin 10 years; travelling twin 17 years
Earth twin 10 years; travelling twin 6.0 years
questions.explanation: In Earth's frame the round trip is 8.0 light-years at 0.80c, taking 8.0/0.80 = 10 years. The traveller's clock records proper time, 10 × 0.60 = 6.0 years. Swapping the results ignores which twin changes frames, and dividing by 0.60 gives 17 years.

questions.stem: A ladder with a proper length of 10 m moves at 0.60c, where √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.80, towards a barn that is 8.0 m long in its own frame. Which statement is correct?
options: In the barn's frame the ladder is 8.0 m long; in the ladder's frame the barn is 6.4 m long
In both frames the ladder is 8.0 m long and the barn is 8.0 m long
In the barn's frame the ladder is 12.5 m long; in the ladder's frame the barn is 10 m long
In the barn's frame the ladder is 8.0 m long; in the ladder's frame the barn is 10 m long
questions.explanation: Each object is contracted in the frame where it moves. The barn frame measures the ladder as 10 × 0.80 = 8.0 m, so it just fits. The ladder frame measures the barn as 8.0 × 0.80 = 6.4 m, so it does not. Dividing by 0.80 gives a longer, dilated length, which never happens to lengths.

questions.stem: In the ladder-in-the-barn paradox, the farmer says both barn doors were shut at the same instant with the ladder inside. The ladder's frame says the barn is too short. How is this resolved?
options: The ladder is crushed, so it is shorter in both frames when the doors are shut
Length contraction applies only in the barn's frame, so the ladder's frame is mistaken
The barn expands in the ladder's frame, so the ladder fits in both frames
The doors shutting are simultaneous in the barn's frame but not in the ladder's frame
questions.explanation: In the ladder's frame, the far door shuts and reopens before the near door shuts, so the ladder is never fully enclosed. Both frames agree on what happens at each door; they disagree only on the timing of separated events. The paradox is resolved by the relativity of simultaneity.
